transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-27
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Olivia (Redwood AE), Luis (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood Product), Jared (Mistwood Head of Platform), Priya (Mistwood Sec Arch), Tomás (Mistwood Network), Sara (Mistwood ML)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough): Customer evaluating private deployment options. Wants private connectivity with strict egress and data residency. Plan: send diagrams and SOC2 docs, schedule deeper tech workshop.

[00:00] Olivia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Olivia from Redwood. Quick quick intro round?
[00:08] Jared: Jared here, Head of Platform at Mistwood. We're looking into hosting model inference behind our VPC for a couple critical apps.
[00:14] Priya: Priya, security architect. My main thing is, we cannot have customer payloads leaving our VPC or go through public internet endpoints.
[00:21] Tomás: Tomás, network. I'll be configuring peering or transit.
[00:25] Sara: Sara, ML infra — concerned about latency for inference and orchestration with our pipeline.
[00:31] Olivia: Awesome. Luis, do you want to kick to the technical constraints?
[00:35] Luis: Yep. So high level, Mistwood is deciding between Redwood Hosted (with egress protections), Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity) and Redwood Private (VPC deployment). Today we'll zero in on Private: how we connect — peering, PrivateLink/private endpoints, and region placement.
[00:50] Jared: Correct. We have two main constraints: 1) Data residency — inference must stay in our VPC in us-east-1, and 2) Egress control — firewalling, IDS, allowed CIDRs.
[00:59] Priya: Also need audit logs and KMS integration for model keys.
[01:03] Maya: Noted. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs; we can share the SOC2 packet.
[01:10] Tomás: Quick question, does Redwood use AWS PrivateLink or are you doing VPC peering? We prefer PrivateLink for cross-account minimal route table churn.
[01:20] Luis: Great question. Both are supported. Typical pattern is: for hub-and-spoke orgs we recommend Transit Gateway + PrivateLink endpoints for service access — that gives you central egress control. For single-account deployments peering can be simplest, but peering has limitations across overlapping CIDRs and scale.
[01:38] Jared: We're multi-account with a transit hub; that sounds promising. Can you walk through the flow end-to-end?
[01:44] Luis: Sure. Option A: Redwood deploys a private endpoint in your VPC (PrivateLink). You create an interface endpoint in the account where your app runs, and route requests privately over the endpoint to Redwood's service. No internet gateway needed. Option B: If you want Redwood-managed instances inside your VPC, we can deploy the inferencing nodes as an AWS account owned by Mistwood — kind of like bring-your-own VPC private deployment — then traffic stays entirely in your account. Option C: Peering to a Redwood VPC, but that requires non-overlapping CIDR and route propagation on TGW.
[02:17] Priya: For Option B, if Redwood instances are in our account, who manages patching and SLAs?
[02:23] Olivia: In that model we deliver the Private package: our control plane is a private control plane that talks to the runtime in your account — Redwood provides the runtime, handles updates, but credentials and keys remain under your control. We can add an enterprise support SLA.
[02:35] Sara: Latency-wise, will PrivateLink add a lot compared to peering?
[02:40] Luis: PrivateLink is typically slightly higher p99 than peering because of the interface endpoint hops, but it's more operationally simple and easier with cross-account. For most inference workloads p99 diffs are small — 10-20ms in many cases — but depends on region and AZ affinity. If you're doing sync low-latency token-by-token workloads, we can benchmark.
[03:00] Tomás: We run a lot of east-west traffic through the Transit Gateway. Will we need to alter route tables or add specific propagation entries?
[03:07] Luis: Yes, you'll need to either create the interface endpoint in the spoke account and ensure it resolves to the Redwood endpoint via private DNS, or if using peering/TGW, configure route propagation so traffic knows to go to the Redwood VPC. We'll provide sample CloudFormation/terraform.
[03:20] Jared: Another compliance question — can we lock down egress so only certain subnets can reach Redwood, and everything else blocked?
[03:26] Priya: (overlapping) We want NAT/gateway egress to be tightly controlled.
[03:29] Maya: You can scope endpoints to specific subnets and security groups; also azure or google equivalents. For egress, common pattern: route outbound model calls through a dedicated egress VPC or use VPC endpoint policies to restrict which principals call the interface endpoint.
[03:45] Tomás: For high throughput batches, will we need to open any ephemeral port ranges?
[03:50] Luis: No unusual ephemeral ranges beyond standard TLS ports. However if you run batch jobs collocated in your account with our runtime there might be internal ports we document. We'll provide the runbook.
[04:01] Jared: Region constraint: we're required to keep workload in us-east-1 for latency and compliance; do you have capacity there for private deployments?
[04:09] Olivia: We do. We maintain private deployments in major regions; us-east-1 is commonly supported. If you need dedicated GPUs we can map instance types and availability in that region and check capacity for a Dedicated or Private install.
[04:20] Priya: KMS — can we bring our own CMK and have Redwood use it for model keys?
[04:25] Luis: Yes, BYOK for KMS is supported in the Private offering. We'll exchange IAM roles and we only get temporary STS access to the keys with explicit least-privilege.
[04:36] Sara: What about SSO and user-level RBAC for the console? We need SAML + SCIM provisioning.
[04:42] Maya: We support SAML/OIDC for the private control plane and SCIM for provisioning. We can integrate with your IdP and map roles.
[04:48] Jared: Any notes on logging? We want all model request logs captured to our SIEM and not persisted by Redwood beyond retention windows.
[04:56] Olivia: In Private you can route logs to your CloudWatch/Stackdriver or S3; we can also configure retention. For Hosted there's additional redaction and retention options but Private gives you full control.
[05:06] Priya: Ok, can you clarify the difference between endpoint policies and security groups? Which is recommended?
[05:12] Luis: Security groups restrict IP/port at the ENI level for interface endpoints. Endpoint policies are IAM resource-based policies that limit which principals can call the endpoint. We recommend using both: SGs for network-level limits and endpoint policies for identity-level access control.
[05:25] Tomás: Our TGW has prefix lists and we use AWS Network Firewall on egress. Will Redwood's PrivateLink flow be compatible?
[05:31] Luis: Yes, PrivateLink sits behind interface endpoints; traffic flows to our service VPC. You can still pass it through TGW and network firewall depending on your setup. If you want full egress inspection we can route via a central egress VPC. We'll include an architecture diagram.
[05:48] Jared: Pricing — does Private incur additional setup or per-endpoint charges we should budget?
[05:53] Olivia: There's an enterprise setup fee and an ongoing usage-based fee. PrivateLink also has AWS endpoint hour and data processing charges; we'll surface an example cost sheet. For Dedicated capacity there's a monthly reserved fee as well.
[06:05] Sara: One of our apps does real-time token streaming for chat. Any notes about streaming over PrivateLink?
[06:11] Luis: Streaming over PrivateLink works; keep an eye on MTU and idle timeouts for interface endpoints. We can tune chunk size and keepalive.
[06:20] Priya: Slight tangent — are there any known multicast or UDP requirements?
[06:24] Luis: No, everything is over HTTPS/TLS (TCP). No UDP required.
[06:28] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[06:30] Jared: Let's talk failover — if a Redwood AZ goes down in us-east-1, do you failover across regions or AZs?
[06:36] Olivia: For Private we recommend a multi-AZ deployment inside the same region for HA. Cross-region failover is possible but adds complexity; some customers keep a warm standby in another region. We can propose an HA topology.
[06:48] Tomás: How do we validate network paths? Can we run end-to-end connectivity tests?
[06:52] Luis: Yes, we provide a connectivity test tool and we'll run a sample inference with a small model to validate both latency and routing. We can also provide pcap-level traces if your team needs them.
[07:03] Priya: Any thoughts on IP addressing? We have tight allocation.
[07:06] Luis: If using PrivateLink, interface endpoints consume ENI IPs from subnets you choose — often a /28 is enough for small scale, but we'll size based on expected concurrency. If deploying Redwood nodes into your account you'll need a larger /24-ish depending on fleet size.
[07:22] Sara: Ok — for benchmarking, we want to test both p99 latency and cost per token. Can Redwood run a week-long perf run?
[07:30] Olivia: Yes. We can spin up a temporary bench harness in your account or route traffic to a test private endpoint. We'll capture token breakdown, latency percentiles, and token cost.
[07:40] Jared: On compliance, Priya — any blocker you see from what's described so far?
[07:44] Priya: So far it's fine; my two items are: 1) need SOC2 and proof of least-priv access for keys, 2) egress controls and retention policies in writing. If Redwood can provide those docs we'll be comfortable moving to an architecture workshop.
[07:58] Olivia: We'll send the SOC2 packet and a red-team network security doc.
[08:03] Luis: I'll also attach sample terraform to create the interface endpoint, security groups, and DNS entries.
[08:09] Tomás: For the DNS, do you recommend private DNS enabled on the endpoint so my clients resolve to the private address automatically?
[08:15] Luis: Yes, that is the usual pattern. We commonly advise enabling private DNS and creating zone overrides if you have split-horizon DNS. We'll document caveats.
[08:24] Jared: Anything about cross-account role trust? We want clear least-privilege trust boundaries.
[08:30] Maya: We'll exchange cross-account IAM role ARNs; Redwood will only assume those roles via STS for runtime ops. We'll document exactly which permissions are needed.
[08:40] Speaker 2 (customer): Quick — if we use Transit Gateway, will route tables explode?
[08:44] Luis: You can minimize route table entries by using prefix lists and route propagation; but yes TGW introduces more route objects. For large scale we usually recommend PrivateLink in combination with TGW to keep the route tables stable.
[08:57] Jared: Let's wrap with explicit next steps — Olivia?
[09:01] Olivia: Action items as discussed: I'll send diagrams, SOC2 packet and the terraform snippets. We'll also propose dates for the deeper network workshop.
[09:09] Priya: Please include an explicit statement about log retention and KMS BYOK workflow in the SOC packet.
[09:15] Olivia: Will do.

[09:18] (discussion continues with some clarifying Q/A — timestamps omitted for brevity)

[28:35] Luis: To summarize technical options again: 1) Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for minimal cross-account config and best operational isolation; 2) Peering if you prefer direct L3 routing and want minimal added infra; 3) Deploy Redwood runtime inside your account for maximal control where we operate the runtime but keys and logs are yours.
[28:54] Jared: Sounds good. For cost and capacity we need a spreadsheet — what do you need from us?
[28:59] Olivia: Number of concurrent requests, average sequence length, and expected qps/p95 targets. Also whether you want dedicated GPU types (e.g. A10G/V100) or CPU xlarge for embeddings.
[29:12] Sara: We'll share a sample workload and some historical QPS.
[29:16] Priya: Also security contact point for the docs is me.
[29:20] Olivia: Great. We'll target sending everything by EOD 4/30 and propose workshop dates for week of 5/4.

[51:45] Olivia: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifact bundle and calendar invite.
[51:51] Jared: Thanks all.
[51:53] (call ends)
